sections.h2: The keyword universe your tool refuses to show you
body: Gujarat produces a very large share of India's chemicals, dyes and dye intermediates, and the GIDC estates ringing Ahmedabad — Vatva, Naroda, Odhav, Narol, Changodar — are full of manufacturers whose websites consist of a company profile, a contact form and a downloadable catalogue.

Meanwhile, the person who would buy from them is searching something like `108-95-2` or "sodium lauryl sulphate technical grade supplier India". CAS Registry Numbers are how the chemical world unambiguously names a substance, and procurement staff type them constantly because a product name is ambiguous and a CAS number never is.

Every keyword tool will report near-zero volume on those queries. The tools are not lying, exactly — they're extrapolating from clickstream panels that contain almost no industrial procurement behaviour. What they report as zero is often a handful of searches a month by exactly the people who sign purchase orders.
The response is structural, not editorial. You need one indexable page per product, and each page needs to carry every way a buyer might name the thing.
bullets: **CAS number**, in text, in the title and in the body — plus the EC number and HS code where relevant.
**Every synonym**: IUPAC name, common trade name, the abbreviation your industry uses, and the two spellings that differ between British and American English.
**Grade and specification** — technical, LR, AR, USP/BP/EP/IP, food grade, electronic grade — because "grade" is the single most common qualifier in these queries.
**Physical specs as HTML text**: assay percentage, appearance, solubility, packing sizes. A specification table rendered as an image is invisible to a crawler.
**Application and downstream use** — which is how buyers search when they know the problem but not the molecule.
**Documentation** — MSDS/SDS and COA available on request, stated on the page, because that phrase is itself a query.

callout.title: This is programmatic SEO, and there's a line
callout.body: Three hundred product pages generated from a spreadsheet with only the name swapped is scaled content abuse, and Google will suppress the whole domain, not just those pages. The version that works has genuinely distinct specification data on every page. We treat this as [programmatic SEO](/services/programmatic-seo-services), not as a content mill, and the difference is whether each page could stand alone as useful.

sections.h2: Pharma content that survives regulatory review
body: Ahmedabad is one of India's densest pharmaceutical clusters — Zydus, Torrent and Intas are all headquartered here, and the API, intermediates, excipients and contract manufacturing layer around them is deep.

The recurring failure on pharma accounts isn't SEO. It's that marketing writes a page, regulatory affairs rejects it, six weeks disappear, and the page ships gutted of everything that made it rank. The fix is to write to the constraint from the first draft.

In practice that means: no efficacy or cure claims for anything covered by the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, no comparative claims against a named competitor product, no dosage guidance on a public page, and every technical claim traceable to a document you can produce in an audit.

What you can say — and what buyers actually search — is factual and abundant: approval status, inspection history, GMP certifications, DMF and CEP filings, capacity, dosage forms handled, containment level, analytical capability. That list is a content plan, and none of it will get rejected.

callout.title: One workflow change that saves months
callout.body: Put regulatory in the outline review, not the final review. Approving a bulleted outline takes an hour. Approving a finished 1,400-word page takes three rounds and a fortnight, and the page ships late and weaker.

sections.h2: GIFT City: a search market that's still thin
body: GIFT City in Gandhinagar, half an hour from Ahmedabad, is India's only operational International Financial Services Centre, regulated by IFSCA. It has pulled in banking units, fund managers, aircraft and ship leasing, bullion trading and a fast-growing set of advisory firms.

The searchable demand around it is unusually favourable right now, for a boring reason: the rules are new, they change often, and almost nobody has written a clear explanation of any of them. Queries like IFSC banking unit setup, GIFT City AIF registration, family office in GIFT City, or the tax treatment of a fund domiciled there are being typed by people with real budgets, and the results are mostly law-firm PDFs and press releases.

This is a window, not a permanent condition. A firm that publishes genuinely accurate explainers now — dated, versioned, and updated when IFSCA changes a circular — can hold those positions before the larger consultancies notice. The maintenance discipline is the whole game: a regulatory explainer that's eighteen months stale is worse than no page, because it damages the credibility the page was built to establish.

sections.h2: Gujarati, and where it actually matters
body: Gujarati is the state language and it shows up in search exactly where you'd expect: local retail, home services, clinics, education, property, and anything a family decides on together. It shows up almost nowhere in chemical, pharma or IFSC search, because those buyers work in English all day.

The same keyboard pattern applies here as elsewhere in India. Native-script Gujarati queries exist, but transliterated Gujarati and Gujarati-English mixing are far more common, because that's what a phone produces without the user configuring anything.

So the sensible sequence is unglamorous: pull your own Search Console query export, find the transliterated phrasings already reaching your pages, work them into the copy, and reserve full Gujarati-script pages for consumer categories with real volume. We walk through that decision in [English vs regional-language SEO](/compare/english-vs-regional-language-seo).

sections.h2: Denim and D2C: your worst competitor is your own listing
body: Ahmedabad's textile history is the reason the city was once called the Manchester of India, and denim is still one of the things it does at world scale. A generation of D2C apparel and lifestyle brands has grown out of that supply chain.

Those brands hit a specific and infuriating problem. Someone searches your brand name plus a product, and the top result is your Amazon or Myntra listing — not your own site. You still get the sale, at a marketplace commission you didn't need to pay, and you lose the customer's email address permanently.

It happens because marketplace domains carry enormous authority and their product pages are structurally excellent: reviews, schema, images, price, availability. Your product page usually has none of that.

The countermeasures are specific and unexciting. Product schema with real price and availability. Review markup fed by genuinely collected reviews. Unique product copy rather than the supplier description you also gave the marketplace. Category pages built around how people search rather than how your warehouse is organised. And enough brand-level content that your own domain outranks a listing for your own name. We've written that argument out in full at [SEO vs marketplace selling](/compare/seo-vs-marketplace-selling).

faqs.q: Do CAS number searches really have enough volume to bother with?
faqs.a: Keyword tools report near-zero volume for most CAS numbers because their clickstream panels contain almost no industrial procurement behaviour. The searches happen anyway. For a chemical exporter, a handful of monthly searches from buyers who issue tenders is worth more than a five-figure head term you'll never convert.

faqs.q: Isn't a page per chemical product just thin content?
faqs.a: It is if you generate three hundred pages from a spreadsheet with only the name swapped — that's scaled content abuse and it risks the whole domain. It isn't if each page carries genuinely distinct specifications, synonyms, grades, applications and documentation. The test is whether one page would be useful on its own.

faqs.q: How do you write pharma content that regulatory will approve?
faqs.a: Write to the constraint from the outline stage. No efficacy or cure claims covered by the Drugs and Magic Remedies Act, no comparative claims against named products, no public dosage guidance. Build content around approvals, inspection history, GMP status, DMF and CEP filings, capacity and analytical capability — all searched, all approvable.

faqs.q: Do I need a Gujarati version of my website?
faqs.a: For local retail, clinics, property and home services it can be worth it. For chemicals, pharma, IFSC advisory or export B2B it almost never is, because those buyers work in English. Even in consumer categories, most Gujarati-language search arrives transliterated into Roman script rather than in native Gujarati script.

faqs.q: Why does Amazon outrank my own D2C site for my own brand name?
faqs.a: Marketplace domains carry enormous authority and their product pages are structurally strong — reviews, schema, price, availability, images. Most brand product pages have none of that plus duplicated supplier copy. Fixing product schema, collecting your own reviews and writing unique product copy usually reverses it within a quarter.
